courses.course_name: English 9: Foundations of Language and Literature
courses.description: English 9 includes three units of study that reinforce the exploration, relevance, and critical analysis of the following themes: Labels, Labeling, and the Impact of Naming; Storytelling Tropes (like the Hero’s Journey) and Subverting The Tropes; and Conflicts and Connections (Compare and Contrast). Units consist of modern and classic literature along with the teaching and practice of specific writing genres including Informational/Explanatory, Argument Techniques and Narrative Techniques through writer’s workshops, journals, On-demand prompts, and a variety of other mediums. Within each unit, students will participate in various discussions, create, read, compose, and find who they are as learners. Independent Reading- In addition to the required readings and student choice, students will select books from a variety of library lists including, but not limited to: Ultimate Reads, Best Fiction, Quick Reads, Community Book Discussion and many more. Within both semesters of this one-year course, there will be student-led choice of various texts.

courses.description: Building on English 9’s focus on self-discovery, English 10 expands students’ understanding of identity by looking at the ways in which our identity is linked to our sense of power or agency, to act in the world. Students will be introduced to the concept of narrative identity and explore and deepen their understanding of agency, social status, and privilege. Students will be challenged to further their knowledge of the elements of an author’s writing style and their analysis of how those choices create meaning to help the author achieve their purpose for writing. Working both as readers and writers of complex texts, students will be challenged to compare and synthesize across texts, compose essays on demand, and discuss interpretations in dialogue with peers to ensure their preparation to reach their future goals. Independent Reading- In addition to the required readings and student choice, students will select books from a variety of library lists including, but not limited to: Ultimate Reads, Best Fiction, Quick Reads, Community Book Discussion and many more. Within both semesters of this one-year course, there will be student-led choice of various texts.

courses.description: AP Language and Composition is a college-level rhetoric and composition class that develops the ability of students to do the following: read critically and evaluate sources of information to meet the expectations of higher education; fulfill the civic responsibilities of our democracy; and discover the beauty of our world. As readers, students learn the structures and purposes of non-fiction texts applying their understanding as writers through inquiry, explanation, criticism, and argumentation. The understanding of language and texts students gain, leads to significant growth in skill and confidence in writing. Students also expand their literary knowledge by reading classics and poetry as they explore topics including American myth and identity, economic power, race, gender and society, and the relationship between humans and nature.

courses.description: AP Literature and Composition is a college-level literature and composition class. Students will focus on big ideas related to character, setting, structure, narration, figurative language, and literary argumentation. As a result of the extensive reading, students will experience classics and contemporary works that are often mentioned on the exam and will be given detailed instruction on how to write appropriate responses to literature at the AP level. Formal essay assignments on major works will further develop their analytical and interpretive skills. Topics covered: the power of storytelling; identity and power; the nature of tragedy; fate and free will; personal freedoms, and social issues.

courses.description: Speculative fiction, a term first used by Robert A. Heinlein in 1947, encompasses various genres that “speculate” about imagined worlds. In this course, students will survey branches of speculative fiction such as fantasy, dystopian, and science fiction, exploring their respective conventions. The course will delve into the role of technology, magic, armageddon, and more in literature from the 19th century to the present day. Additionally, students will consider how this literature reflects and deflects from reality.

courses.description: This semester-long course surveys and explores our history through the many forms of literature used for protest from novels and speeches to art and film. Students will study issues relevant and important to them in the context of historic and current systems of injustice and the civic and democratic ideals of America’s founding freedom and liberty for all. Students will learn how prejudice based on race, class, and gender formed and consider its impact on individuals, groups, and society. Students will examine multiple factors that impact marginalized groups and how those groups led movements for social change. This course will create opportunities for students to gain a greater understanding of varying perspectives and experiences of people throughout the United States. Students will develop high level critical thinking, reading, research and composition skills and have the opportunity to apply their knowledge and skills as they collaborate to act on an issue of concern to Vermonters and our nation.

courses.description: Students explore the literature of war considering how it reflects the values and beliefs as individuals and as a nation as well as the responsibility we have as citizens especially as it relates to the impact of war on soldiers. Students develop their critical reading skills studying and comparing the many types of texts used to tell war stories including novels, short stories, photos, poetry, film, and non-fiction texts. Students further their inquiry skills in research projects on topics they choose. The projects challenge students to understand and explain the factors that lead to war, to effectively evaluate sources, and to explore many perspectives before drawing conclusions. Discussions are an anchor for learning in class. They ensure students understand how to listen and engage in civil discourse exploring current and timeless topics related to war and violence as well as healing and reconciliation.

courses.description: Students in this course will engage with stories that have been adapted into some sort of retelling, whether it be for stage, screen, or other revitalized formats. We will read and view adaptations of ancient stories (such as Greek mythology and fairy tales) and famous plays (such as Shakespeare), as well as assorted short stories (such as “Supertoys Last All Summer Long”) and choice novels. In addition to critiquing the similarities and differences between the originals and the adaptations, student will consider key ideas in literary analysis such as how some pieces of literature can reflect and comment upon the society from whence they came and also how some pieces of literature hold timeless life lessons that are equally relevant in our world today. Through writing, discussions, and various projects such as creating unique adaptations of transformed source materials themselves, students will engage with the art of adaptation as a powerful facet of storytelling.

courses.course_name: Social Issues in Young Adult Literature
courses.description: Young adult literature has increasingly become a vehicle for young people to explore social issues. As students explore themes including the myriad ways people experience justice and belonging, they will build the skills to plan and facilitate Socratic Seminar discussions, taking ownership of the direction of the class. Key topics may include mental health, substance abuse, family, community, identity, violence and justice, immigration and home. As young adults studying young adult literature, students will consider what conclusions can be made about power, the individual in society, and the nature of community through these works.

courses.description: Students will explore Gothic literature and its influence on the mystery and horror genres. Through close examinations of several texts, we will identify the unique aspects of each genre in addition to their commonalities. Beware of ghosts, murderers, and monsters as we seek to understand all things that go bump in the night. Students will also identify the themes and common Gothic tropes utilized by genres such as: mystery, thriller, horror, science fiction, and fantasy and determine what truths are revealed about human nature and society. Some film presentations will also be analyzed, focusing on the translation from print to film.

courses.description: Spend a quarter exploring current Young Adult Reads for next year’s Community Book Discussion list. Read from award winning books and share your findings with the rest of the class. Read from your favorite genres and try new ones! It’s up to you!

Spend a quarter exploring your interests by reading books that matter to you. Put together a list of books that you want to read and knock them out one at a time. Become an expert on vampire literature or figure out what makes an excellent graphic novel. Read different fantasy novels and understand how to make an imaginary world or discover Victorian England. Tackle the classics; prepare for AP courses and college reading. You will read and share your findings with the rest of the class. Read from one genre or across a range of genres! It’s up to you! Just read, read, and read some more, and then share it with the world.

courses.description: Spend a quarter completing your college application, college essays, and college mini-essays before your college deadline. This nine-week course is structured as a writing workshop where you will make goals weekly to accomplish the day you hit “submit.”

In this course, students strengthen their writing skills by learning how to express their ideas and experience in convincing, meaningful, and beautiful ways. Students will develop their understanding of different structures and forms and how they support an author’s purpose in writing. They will analyze model texts, practice writing in different genres, and develop their capacity to give and receive feedback on writing. This will prepare students to develop a piece of writing that they will publish as part of their final project. Throughout the course, they will consider the questions: How do audience and purpose influence writing? What are the differences between drafting, revising, and editing? How can I engage my readers’ attention? Students read and discuss examples of effective writing as a way to hone their skills. At the end of the course, students participate in a public reading or public publishing as part of the final exam.

Literacy Lab provides a systematic and structured reading approach that will help students improve in the areas of comprehension and fluency. Our primary focus in the program is to ensure that students have an opportunity to read with competence, confidence, and understanding. Daily, students monitor their fluency rate, comprehension, and crucial reading skills (vocabulary expansion, fact and opinion, sequence of events, inferences, and main idea) as well as their growth, mastery, and areas that desire improvement. Throughout the year – different genres are addressed, writing on self-selected topics, and question-response sessions are incorporated. Formal assessment is administered to all students in the program (pre and post testing) in order to identify strengths and weaknesses. Assessment scores are shared with parents, the student, and the academic team for accountability. Students who enroll in this program learn to celebrate reading and learn more about the world.

courses.description: Global Studies 9 takes a thematic approach to teaching key concepts and developments throughout human history. The two main themes explored in GS9 include the interaction between humans and the environment, and the development and interaction of cultures. The curriculum consists of five units of study, each embedded with a variety of tasks that develop our learners’ capacity toward critical thinking, coordination and collaboration, inquiry skills, history, geography, civic and economic knowledge, as well as the development of research, technology, and public speaking skills.

We aim to recognize, understand, and appreciate the perspectives and world views of others. We communicate ideas effectively with diverse audiences by engaging in open, appropriate, and effective interactions across cultures. Lastly, we will take action for collective well-being and sustainable development both locally and globally.

Core themes include economic growth, rights and reform, cultural change, movement of people, and foreign policy and conflict. Through examining past events and their impact on today’s world, students will form their own definition of citizenship and justice.

The course is designed to give students factual knowledge and analytic skills necessary to critically deal with the materials and problems in United States history. The program prepares students for intermediate and advanced college courses by making demands upon them equivalent to those made by full-year introductory college courses. All students are expected to take at least one AP exam. The cost of the AP exam is approximately $98. This may be used to meet the Grade 11 United States History requirement.

courses.description: A.P. Psychology is an exploration into the human mind. Why do we think the things that we think? Why do we do the things that we do? Do we change over time or stay the same? Are we a product of nature or nurture? While these questions and many others like it will be examined, this course is designed to introduce students to the systematic and scientific study of the behavior and mental processes of human beings and other animals. Students will be exposed to the psychological facts, principles, and phenomena associated with each of the major subfields within psychology. Students will also learn about the ethics and methods psychologists use in their science and practice.

courses.description: This course, which will prepare a student for the Advanced Placement Exam, provides an analytical perspective on government and politics in the United States. The course will include both the study of general concepts used to interpret U.S politics as well as specific case studies. The various institutions, groups, beliefs and ideas that constitute U.S. political reality will be explored. The following specific topics will be studied: Constitutional Underpinnings of the U.S. Government, Political Beliefs and Behaviors, Political Parties and Interest Groups, Institutions of the National Government, Public Policy, Civil Rights and Civil Liberties. All AP students are expected to take at least one AP exam.

courses.description: Criminal Justice is a nine-week elective course that examines the U.S. criminal justice system. Topics of study will include the constitutional foundations of the legal system, methods of investigation, the criminal court process, theories and types of punishment, and the juvenile justice system. Explorations of various careers in the criminal justice system will be a part of the course. Students will have the opportunity to explore topics of interest, and the class may elect to conduct a mock trial.

courses.description: At times, the subject economics has been termed the dismal science, but economics is anything but dismal as we make many economic decisions regularly. Economics is about human behavior, especially how people choose to use resources. In this course we will examine some principles of economics through a modern lens of knowledge, technology, entrepreneurship, and innovation. This course will examine what is needed for economic growth and how new ideas, new technology and entrepreneurial skills work in today’s world.

Geography is divided into two main branches: Human geography and physical geography. Human Geography is the study of people in place, including the various political, economic, and social factors that create place. Physical Geography studies the processes and patterns in our natural environment. Human geography and physical geography provide an opportunity to examine how humans interact with their environment and how the surrounding environment can impact people. This course is designed to explore geographic processes, such as the physical and human systems that shape our world, and geographic tools, such as maps, geospatial technology, and other forms of data. Geography is a semester-long social studies elective available to 11th and 12th-grade students.

There is more than one way to study and engage in history. History through Film offers an exciting opportunity to access historical narratives and social trends by screening films, analyzing their content and messages, and using film as a springboard to authentic socio-political discourse. In addition to screening films from around the world, students will engage in Socratic discussion, research historical accuracy, and collaborate to better understand some of the cultural, religious, political, and social movements of human history.

Philosophy means the “love of wisdom.” In this class students have the opportunity to further develop their sense of wonder. What makes an action right or wrong? Who am I? What is the meaning of life? What makes a word mean anything? How can we know if there is anything outside of our own minds? People’s analytical capacities are highly developed before a great deal about the world is known. Many people start to think about philosophical problems on their own—about what really exists, or whether we can know anything. The main concern of this class is to question, argue, try out new ideas, and find understanding about common ideas that all people use every day.

Applied Psychology will take students on an exploration of the many ways that psychology is part of their everyday lives. Psychological research underlies many areas of life that impact people and this class will address how issues such as money, the law, sports, health, technology, school, work and family are influenced by the study and application of modern psychology. Psychology is a diverse field that has much to offer society in terms of both theoretical and practical knowledge. Students will change the way they think about themselves and the world around them as they apply the practical concepts from this course.

The goal of Personal Finance is to help students become financially responsible and conscientious members of society. This course develops students' understanding and skills in such areas as career selection, budgeting, proficiency in student and auto loans, the wise use of credit, and the understanding of how to invest in various securities. This course will give students the tools and resources needed to make wise financial decisions. Students will analyze their personal financial decisions, evaluate the costs and benefits of their decisions, and apply the knowledge learned to financial situations encountered later in life. This course will provide a foundational understanding for making informed personal financial decisions.

One focus of this course is on civic and political institutions, specifically, how the U.S. Constitution establishes a system of government that has powers, responsibilities, and limits that have changed over time and that are still contested. The second focus of this course is processes, rules, and laws. Students will analyze how people use and challenge local, state, and national laws to address a variety of public issues. Students will also analyze historical, contemporary, and emerging means of changing societies, promoting the common good, and protecting rights. This course is complemented by the frequent aid of elected and public officials to enrich course content.

Students will be given the tools to critically understand and evaluate statistical conclusions, to be able to interpret the validity of the information they will encounter in everyday life. courses.description: In the first unit students use mathematical and computer models to determine the factors that affect the size and diversity of populations in ecosystems, including the availability of resources and interactions between organisms. In the second unit students make a model that links photosynthesis and respiration in organisms to cycles of energy and matter in the Earth system. They gather evidence about the linked history of Earth’s biosphere and atmosphere. They also explore the macronutrients in our diet and the energy transformations that occur as they eat and process food. The third and fourth units focus on how organisms grow, maintain themselves, and pass along genetic information. In the fifth unit students develop a model about how rock layers record evidence of evolution as fossils. Building on their learning from previous grades, they focus on effectively communicating this evidence and relate it to principles of natural selection. The final unit focuses on ecosystem stability and the response to climate change. Required of all 9th graders. This is a Lab Science.

This survey course exposes students to some of the major concepts that they will encounter in the physical/earth sciences course of study. Through problems that engage and challenge, students explore a broad range of affiliated topics, including forces and motion, Earth’s system, geology, climate change, waves, and the origin of the universe. The course applies and concurrently develops secondary level knowledge and skills in mathematics, science, engineering, and technology. Required of all 10th graders. This is a Lab Science.

courses.description: Chemistry is the third foundational course designed to provide the chemistry and earth science background necessary to understand the effect of human action on local and global climate. Chemistry topics include the structure of matter, the relationship between the subatomic structure of matter and the properties that matter exhibits, conservation of matter and energy, chemical reactions, and nuclear reactions. Earth science topics include atmospheric composition, the greenhouse effect and the way matter cycles in the environment (especially the carbon cycle). In addition to understanding why environmental problems like climate change are occurring, students will analyze potential solutions. This is a Lab Science.

courses.description: The AP Biology course is designed to be the equivalent of an introductory biology course usually taken by biology majors during their first 2 semesters of college. The goals of the course are to prepare students for a college level workload, while building college level lab-science skills and to develop college-level content knowledge. However, extensive high school supports are offered to help students build success. Students who are interested in pursuing biology careers may earn college credit with a score of 3, 4, or 5 on the May exam which will allow them to begin college with higher-level classes. However, most students looking to major in biology choose to take intro biology classes in college and find this a perfect course to prepare them to excel in those classes. Students pursuing other science majors or non-science majors should consider AP biology as a way to demonstrate college level skills in diverse fields and earn college credits to satisfy college liberal arts requirements. During the first semester, students study biochemistry and cellular biology. The second semester explores genetics, evolution, and ecology. Students will spend approximately 20% of class time engaged in laboratory activities. This class is intended to be taken by juniors or seniors and does not require chemistry as a prerequisite.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of 9th grade science. This is a Lab Science.

All AP students are expected to take at least one AP exam. Students pursuing other science majors or non-science majors should consider AP physics 1 as a way to demonstrate college level skills in diverse fields and earn college credits to satisfy college liberal arts requirements.

courses.description: Food Science is designed to reinforce and enhance your knowledge of scientific principles and processes through the study of foods and nutrition. Within a hands-on lab approach, students will learn the chemistry of cooking. Chemical/biochemical reactions of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and other constituents in fresh and processed foods are discussed with respect to food quality. Reaction conditions and processes that affect color, flavor, texture, nutrition, and safety of food are emphasized.

Passionate researcher, teacher, and author, Ann Wigmore once said, “The food you eat can either be the safest and most powerful form of medicine or the slowest form of poison”. Students will study the vast science and connection involved in growing, preparing, and eating food. The curriculum applies knowledge in plant biology, ecology, chemistry, and environmental science to real systems that students can relate to whether or not they plan to enter into a science-based job or program after high school. These include connections between those who eat and those who produce food, between our own health and the health of our environment, and between what happens in the classroom, the cafeteria, and the community. Student strengths are leveraged to help the group to meet our collective goals. Our goals are to produce a good amount of food for our local community. In addition, our goals are that every student learns more about the food they eat and to see themselves as empowered producers as well as knowledgeable consumers. Activities are mostly outside, mostly hands-on, and entirely completed during class time. As our “lab”, we will use the school garden and growing spaces. Students will never look at food the same way!

courses.description: Introduction to Forensic Science is a nine-week hands-on investigative science course designed to expose students to the field of forensics. In this course students will learn how to apply the processes and technologies of science to problems associated with identifying and analyzing evidence in criminal events. Some of the topics that will be covered will include analysis of fingerprints, DNA, hair and fiber, blood, glass, and soil. A strong emphasis will be placed on developing scientific inquiry principles and skills. This is a Lab Science.

Take your interest in forensic science further. Students will consider additional techniques for collection and analysis of forensic evidence. Students will also take a deeper dive into the science behind blood analysis, chemical analysis and illuminate the many uses of DNA evidence. We will continue to consider true crime analysis to see how forensic scientists are working in the real world. Students will continue to focus on the scientific method and use of comparison and controls.

courses.description: Want to know how your brain works? Neuroscience is the study of the nervous system and how it regulates behavior. This one-quarter course is designed as a “users manual” to introduce concepts about how your senses communicate with your brain, how your brain communicates with your muscles and how the many parts of your brain communicate with each other. We consider the evolution of the human brain, the differences between the human brain and other animal brains and admire the intelligence of non-human brains. Students will consider the benefits of exercise on our cognitive functions both now and as we age. In addition, we look at the structure of the brain and nervous system and understand the structure of brain cells and how they communicate messages to each other. Students will learn about how we pay attention, why we struggle sometimes to pay attention in class and the brain characteristics commonly known as ADHD. We discuss the effect of stress and anxiety on our brains as well as brain injuries and diseases. Students interested in pursuing biology in college will find this class useful in addition to (either before or after) AP biology and Anatomy and Physiology. However, students who are pursuing non-biology fields in college may also enjoy understanding more about how their brain works (AP biology and Anatomy and Physiology are not required). Students may even be inspired to pursue a career in neuroscience!

courses.description: Want to know EVEN MORE about how your brain works? Students that have completed the Introduction to Neuroscience class may wish to take this follow up class. In addition to going deeper into topics from the Introduction to Neuroscience class, in this course, we will also consider: ● the impacts of food, medicines and drugs on the brain’s function. ● what happens to our brains as we sleep and dream ● parasites that can infect our brains ● Short term and long-term memory formation ● Neuroplasticity and how we can change our brain We will continue to learn about how we study the brain including with scientific experimentation as well as with use of new technology. Students interested in pursuing biology in college will find this class useful in addition to (either before or after) AP biology and Anatomy and Physiology. Students will further develop the functional skills necessary to use the Spanish language beyond the classroom. Students should obtain the level of Intermediate Mid (ACTFL) or B1.3 (CEFR) in Spanish by the end of this course.
courses.prerequisites: Grade of B or higher in Spanish IV and a commitment to speaking Spanish is essential.
courses.notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION; *Depending on the enrollment and students’ schedules, Spanish IV and/or Spanish V may be offered every other day for the entire academic year for 1 unit of credit.

courses.description: For students who have successfully completed at least level 1 of the language and would like to intern and assist in a lower-level Spanish class. The duration can range from quarter to year-long and is an individualized plan based on students’ desired outcomes and career goals. Please see your Spanish teacher ahead of time if you are interested.
courses.prerequisites: Strong basic language skills, desire to help others and recommendation of teacher.
courses.notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

courses.description: This course is intended for students who want to gain confidence and improve their fundamental computing skills. We will discuss the history of computers and different computing devices that are commonly used today. Students will work with the most frequently used software tools (email, documents, slideshows, spreadsheets) and learn advanced features that are useful to workflow and productivity. The course will end with a personalized investigation of a professional computer application that connects to our other electives.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

courses.description: This course is intended for college-bound juniors and seniors who are considering a career in computers, math, science and/or engineering. This course will cover the foundations of programming in Java and build into topics such as designing solutions, object-oriented programming, debugging, data structures and abstractions. This is a challenging course that will require you to re-evaluate how you approach and solve problems, but the skills that you gain in computational thinking can be applied to all content areas.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of Algebra II. The motivated student does not need prior programming experience.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art
courses.notes: The AP course and AP Exam must be completed in its entirety for AP credit to appear on your transcript. Early withdrawal will result in no AP credit on the Transcript.

courses.description: This course will cover the basics of creating 2D and 3D digital art and how to develop animations using both styles. This is a project-based course where we will learn by doing. Throughout the course students will develop a portfolio of work that can be easily transferred or shared. No artistic talent is needed to succeed in this course, and we will work to improve your skills at any level.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

courses.description: In this hands-on course we will examine the application of computer-controlled physical systems. We will start with a look at binary counting and its link to electronic systems before diving into basic electrical components. The bulk of this course will focus on using these components as building blocks to mimic simple systems (ex. Automatic door, remote control), and will wrap up with students constructing a complex system of their choice.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

courses.description: Enjoy playing video games, board games or card games? Have you ever wanted to create your own? In this course we will look at the way digital games are created. Students will learn to use Unity, a popular free game engine, to make simple games and the course will finish with students applying their skills to construct a personalized game.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

courses.description: Interested in computer programming but don’t know where to start? This course serves as an introduction to writing code to perform a variety of computer functions. We will cover the foundations of programming including variables, conditional statements, loops, and functions. This course is designed for beginners and will be taught using the Python programming language.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

courses.description: This is the course for students who have completed Computer Literacy and want to gain real-world work experience. This could include assisting with a computer literacy course or working with the school IT department. The students benefit by examining the use of technology from both an educational perspective and a business perspective. Students will be able to gain experience that expands existing skills and may lead to a reference for future work. Independent projects with detailed documentation are also considered. This work will help you stand out from the crowd on your college applications.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

courses.description: Discover the artistic and technical aspects of web design. This course will primarily focus on front-end development using the Big 3 (HTML, CSS and Javascript) to create and style personal websites. We will learn how to write websites from scratch and look at modern tools that can assist the process. By the end of the course students will have developed and launched a webpage.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

courses.description: This course will focus on the art and impact of documentary filmmaking. Students will learn from some of the great documentary filmmakers around the world, covering issues that matter most. The course will balance screening particular powerful documentaries, with learning how to make short documentary films of their own. Students will work collaboratively to seek out local stories, develop story concepts, capture interviews, balance archival footage with new footage, and edit it all together into a powerful piece of new media. This class will culminate with a film festival, and individual DVDs of student projects for college applications. This class is brought to you by the Milton Creative Media Lab.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

courses.description: This is an introductory course to digital filmmaking and is a prerequisite to Filmmaking II as well as a foundation course for those interested in being involved in YJTV. Students will learn the language and skills to create their own short films in this 9-week course using digital HD cameras, gimbals and drones as well as Apple’s Final Cut Pro and Adobe Premier. Students will work individually and in groups to write, direct, light, and edit their own original productions. We will analyze scenes from groundbreaking films, understand the technology of filmmaking today, and work together to entertain and enlighten the world. This class will culminate in a film festival, and individual DVDs of student projects to use in college applications. This class is brought to you by the Milton Creative Media Lab.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

courses.description: This is an advanced course in filmmaking and requires that participants successfully complete Filmmaking I. Students will work in crews to write screenplays, direct, and edit short films using digital HD cameras gimbals and drones, as well as Apples’ Final Cut Pro and Adobe Premiere. The concept of this course is to use this time to create films that we can submit into local and national student film festivals. This class will culminate in a film festival, and individual DVDs of student projects will be provided to use in college applications. This course is brought to you by the Milton Creative Media Lab.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

courses.course_name: Gold Records and Glory: Audio Engineering Technique
courses.description: This is a multi-level audio engineering course designed to teach students how to use digital audio recording technology to make music. Whether you are a trained musician or someone who just loves music, but does not play an instrument, this course is designed for everyone. Students will be introduced to recording technique and theory and work to complete a variety of individual and group projects using Apple’s Garageband, Logic Pro, and the Protools Recording Suite. We will culminate in a listening party and CDs will be made available for participants. This course is brought to you by the Milton Creative Media Lab.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

courses.description: YJTV is an opportunity for students to create a monthly news and variety show to be screened for the entire student body, as well as made available online. This class is for any student interested in camera operation, sound mixing, content editing, or on-air talent such as anchorpersons, weather experts, and sports commentators. This is a unique opportunity for dedicated students to produce a valuable resource to the school and broader community, and to become a star both in front of, and behind the camera. No prior broadcasting experience necessary, however completion of Filmmaking I is a plus. This class is brought to you by the Milton Creative Media Lab.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

courses.description: In this quarter foundational course, students will explore several different artistic media and techniques. The elements and principles of design are studied through drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture, and other media. Projects will incorporate the study of historical and contemporary artists while allowing students freedom to explore their creativity. This course is required for those students desiring to pursue any of the advanced courses offered in the fine arts.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED

courses.description: This quarter course is designed to further the exploration of various media while learning advanced techniques. We will explore drawing, painting, printmaking, and sculpture. The course will focus on developing observational skills while fostering creative imagination. Students will examine the styles of both historical and contemporary American Artists while developing their own personal style of expression.

AP Art is intended for highly motivated students who wish to pursue art in college. Observational drawing will be stressed as students continue to develop personal visual imagery through intensive work in drawing, painting, mixed media, printmaking, and sculpture. As with other art courses, the projects will be based on artists from contemporary and historical times as a springboard for creativity.
courses.notes: The AP course must be completed in its entirety for AP credit. Early withdrawal will result in no AP credit on the Transcript.

courses.description: In this class you will learn about art and artists from the 1400’s to the present. We will discuss these famous works of art and artists in depth, learning about why they made specific works of art and who they were as people. We will also use the techniques these artists used to make art, through our own projects. This class is both a lecture and a hands-on art making experience.

In this quarter course, the student will express him/herself in clay to make functional pottery. Students will explore line, shape, form, color, texture, and pattern as tools of expression and use basic building techniques including pinch, coil, slab, sculpting and wheel.

Clay and Pottery II is an extension of Clay and Pottery I with an emphasis placed on creativity and individual interests. Projects, which may be thrown on the potter's wheel or hand constructed, will include sculptural and functional forms traditional to clay. Experimentation with techniques will be encouraged, as will works of depth and complexity.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of Clay and Pottery I
courses.notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

courses.description: Drawing is highly recommended as a foundation for every type of art. Students will learn about the fundamental skills of drawing. This class will focus on drawing from images, realistic shading, shadow, perspective, etc. We will use different drawing mediums such as pencil, charcoal, ink, as well as digital Procreate.

In this class, we’ll explore the foundations of jewelry making and metalworking. You’ll learn essential techniques like cutting and filing metal, soldering, stone setting, creating linkages, and crafting glass pendants. Along with hands-on projects, you’ll discover the history of jewelry design, and each student will research and present on an influential jewelry designer to share with the class.
courses.prerequisites: One art class or permission of instructor.
courses.notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

courses.description: In this class, we’ll dive into the fundamentals of 3D sculpture using materials like wood, metal, glass, paper, and wire. You’ll explore various techniques, from carving and building forms to fusing glass, bringing your creations to life in three dimensions. Alongside hands-on projects, you’ll also learn about the history of sculpture, and each student will research and present on a notable artist to share insights with the class.
courses.prerequisites: One art class or permission of instructor.
courses.notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

courses.description: In this class, students will develop their painting skills and techniques using watercolor and acrylic paint. Students will explore the style of many artists throughout history, while developing their own paintings. The subjects considered and studied will include landscapes, still-life, the figure, and abstraction.
courses.prerequisites: Art 1
courses.notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

courses.description: Art Studio is an opportunity for students who have taken at least two classes of art to pursue independent work with the support of an Art teacher. Credit will be based on portfolio review.
courses.notes: program

courses.description: This course is designed to appeal to students coming from various musical backgrounds and is a springboard to greater understanding of music. This course explores parts of the guitar, riffs and melodies, open chords, and scale patterns. Students will learn songs that are related to their specific music interests as well as explore basic elements of songwriting with the guitar. This course concentrates on acoustic guitar. Note: Students may bring their own acoustic guitar.

This course focuses on intermediate guitar techniques that include barre chords, fingerstyle, picking, and playing across the fretboards. This course focuses on both acoustic and electric guitar styles. Students will learn chords and melodies in a variety of styles as well as styles that are related to their music interests. Note: Students may bring their own acoustic guitar.
courses.prerequisites: Permission of instructor, completion of Guitar 1 or equivalent mastery of the guitar.
courses.notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

courses.description: Music Theory and Composition is a course designed for motivated students interested in learning about music language: scales, keys, chord structure and harmony. Students will study and analyze musical elements and be given opportunities to compose and arrange their own music.

courses.course_name: Modern Band: Piano, Guitar, Bass, Drums and Vocals
courses.description: Modern Band is a course designed to get students, regardless of experience, involved in music. Throughout this course, students will learn many aspects of music, including how to play multiple musical instruments (guitar, bass, drum set, piano, etc.). Students will be given the opportunity to collaborate musically with one another and perform for others. By the end of this course students will be able to play songs in a rock band style.

This course is designed for students from a variety of musical backgrounds and serves as a foundation for understanding and performing music through the piano. Students will explore essential piano techniques, note reading, rhythm, scales, and chord progressions. The course emphasizes performance, creativity, and personal connection to music. Students will perform individual and ensemble pieces, learn songs relevant to their musical interests, and engage in basic songwriting and composition. Instruction will primarily utilize electric keyboards. This is a beginner level course and no experience is necessary.

This course is an advanced co-curricular offering of the music department. Advanced vocal music will be emphasized. Students will perform at least 4 times per year in a variety of settings. Rehearsals are held outside of school time at least 1 time per week.
courses.prerequisites: Successful vocal audition including sight reading, commitment to weekly rehearsals, and prior Middle School or High School vocal experience.
courses.notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

courses.description: This course is designed to give the student an opportunity to study and perform advanced band literature of various styles. The student will learn to appreciate, to understand, to perform, and to criticize with discrimination within the area of instrumental music. Members from this group may audition for the District, All-State, and New England Music Festivals. The Music Department acknowledges the importance of these music festivals and views them as a reward for excellence and a means to obtain excellence in musicianship. STUDENTS WILL PERFORM AT LEAST THREE TIMES A YEAR. ATTENDANCE AT PERFORMANCES IS MANDATORY.

The Milton High School Chorus is for all students who like or would like to sing. The course is designed for students who wish to extend their knowledge of music through performance of vocal music. Music selections will include a variety of styles stressing regular choral repertoire including classical, spirituals, sacred, madrigals, and pop music. There will also be opportunities for students to do solo and small group work, as well as to audition for and participate in a variety of music festivals. The goals for students who are members of the chorus experience are to learn to sing as a group in multi-part harmony, to develop the ability to read music, to gain an understanding for basic music theory, to gain the knowledge of various styles of music, to perform as often as possible, to contribute to the musical life of the school and community, and to participate in special events and festivals. Homework: Extensive rehearsal and practice - occasional written work. Method of Evaluation: Teacher observation, participation in class and lessons, aural exams, quizzes, and occasional tests.

This course is a performance organization, which explores jazz, pop, and rock music in a small instrumental group. This is a half-credit course, which meets once per week after school. Students must audition to participate.

Students will use a skills based approach to investigate healthy behaviors and environments that impact them, their family, peers, community members, fellow citizens, global citizens and the earth. Using the social-ecological model as a framework, students will identify the multiple levels that influence health behaviors while investigating and analyzing the Youth Risk Behavior data from the MTSD district, the State of Vermont and other reliable sources to determine areas of strength or improvement. Students will also identify reliable sources of information and evidence-based resources that can contribute to decision-making around personal and community health. Students will be able to practice behavioral modification strategies for themselves based on personal reflections and in depth analysis of health factors beyond individual control. As a summative assessment, the students will be afforded the opportunity to interpret data, and advocate for personal, community or political change on a topic of their choosing.
courses.prerequisites: Grade 10
courses.notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

courses.description: The Driver Education course is designed to develop the student driver and teach traffic safety, to assist drivers in the study of traffic crash prevention, and to acquire knowledge and skills leading to the safe operation of motor vehicles. The class consists of classroom instruction and behind-the-wheel driving/observing. Students are required to drive outside of class for at least 20 hours during the course to obtain a “yellow card”. Students should expect to spend about 1 hour outside of class (each week) on reading and various worksheets to enhance their learning. There is a mandatory parent/student meeting near the beginning of the class to help aide parents/students about their roles in this process. Students must have a learner’s permit before the course begins and ideally have 10 hours of driving practice. This is NOT OPEN TO FRESHMEN without the permission of the school counselor. Students can miss a maximum of 8 classes and still meet the attendance requirement; more than 8 classes missed, and students are removed from the class and need to skip a semester before taking the class again.
This course is designed to provide support to students in completing the homework portion of the class and may need extra time to practice skills.
courses.prerequisites: Permission of Driver’s Ed Instructor
courses.notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION; (Students enrolled in Driver Education)

courses.description: This course promotes lifelong fitness, teamwork, and personal well-being. Students will explore fitness concepts, build collaboration skills through team and cooperative games, and develop self-awareness with social-emotional learning (SEL) and mindfulness activities. Non-traditional, low-organization games encourage creativity, inclusion, and fun while enhancing movement skills. By the end of the course, students will understand the value of staying active, building trust and cooperation with others and maintaining a balanced, healthy lifestyle. This class meets everyday for one quarter.
courses.fulfills_text: Required for Grade 9

courses.description: The purpose of this class is to expose students to activities that can lead them toward healthy active lifestyles after high school. Some of the activities may include Archery, Badminton, Basketball, Circuit Training, Cross Country Skiing, Dance, Lawn Games, New Games/Name Games/Trust Activities, Pickleball, Racquetball, Snowshoeing,Tennis, Ultimate Frisbee, Volleyball, Walk/Jog/Run, etc. This class meets every day for one quarter.

The purpose of this class is to offer students opportunities to develop new skills through participation in activities and games. It is our goal to expose students to activities that can lead them toward healthy active lifestyles after high school. Some of the activities that may be used as a vehicle towards fitness and wellness are Archery, Badminton, Basketball, Circuit Training, Cross Country Skiing, Dance, Field Hockey, Flag Football, Floor Hockey, Lacrosse, New Games/Name Games/Trust Activities, Pickleball, Racquetball, Snowshoeing, Soccer, Team Handball, Tennis, Ultimate Frisbee, Volleyball, Walk/Jog/Run, etc. This class is suitable for those with a competitive spirit.

This class is designed for 11th and 12th grade students to dive deeply into the components of fitness and involves academic and hands-on ways to achieve personal fitness. The students will be assessing, refining, and maintaining a comprehensive personal fitness plan based on personal performance on a nationally recognized fitness assessment. They will show knowledge of physiological effects and adjust their physical activity to achieve the physiological response. Through class discussions, readings, hands on experience and reflections the students will learn how to implement the four components of fitness into their lives.
courses.notes: Prose says designed for 11th and 12th grade students; offerings list shows 10-12

courses.description: The objective of this course is to prepare students to be coaches. Each Student will have the opportunity to engage in hypothetical and real situations that arise when coaching sports and activities. Students will have the chance to analyze and discuss topics involved in coaching that include coaching certifications, gender, culture, sportsmanship, ethics, officiating/refereeing, careers in sports, and building and implementing practice plans. Students will gain knowledge from experienced coaches through guest speakers, interviews, and/or mentoring. Students may also have the opportunity to coach a youth sport during the class, and work toward collecting community service hours. This class will have some in-class lessons, as well as lessons in the gymnasium and on the fields. The goal of this class is for each student to leave with one or more coaching certifications, a coaching resume, and hands-on experience.

Students will enjoy a very welcoming and non-competitive atmosphere during this experience. The class will focus on health, fitness, and wellness implementation to create a symbiotic and harmonious relationship with the mind, body, and soul. Students will have the opportunity to take part in breathing exercises, mindfulness, meditation, mobility, moving meditation, Pilates, low aerobic intensity, and impact exercises, embracing nature, wellness goals and plans, some non-competitive fun activities, and nutrition information. The overall goal of this course is to create an alternative to traditional PE class and allow students to embark on a personal journey toward holistic health and well-being. This class will focus on the dimensions of wellness that include, but are not limited to, physical, social, emotional, spiritual, intellectual, environmental, and occupational wellness.

This physical education program integrates students of all abilities into the gym for sports, fitness, and other physical activities. The goal is to foster inclusion, build friendships, develop athletic skills, and promote a school-wide culture of understanding and acceptance by providing a shared, positive experience. The model focuses on teamwork and meaningful participation for all students, using rule modifications and higher-ability partners as mentors to ensure success. Examples of activities include basketball, lawn sports, bowling, bocce, dance, general fitness concepts, riding a bike, and other activities that enhance abilities for life now and in the future.
courses.notes: Enrollment capped based on participants.

courses.description: Students who participate in two years of any varsity sport may seek a waiver, which grants them .5 credits for their athletic experience. The waiver request form is available from the guidance office and must be signed by members of the school and athletic administration. Students will be asked to reflect upon their athletic experience through the lenses of both current PE standards and PBGRs to secure the waiver and the associated credit.

Step into the world of 3D design! In this hands-on course, you’ll learn how to bring your ideas to life using modern CAD software, 3D printers, and laser cutters. You’ll design and model your own creations — from custom games to detailed prototypes — while exploring how art, engineering, and technology connect. No experience needed — just your creativity and curiosity. By the end, you’ll have real 3D projects you can hold, share, and be proud of

Ready to take your creativity to the next level? In this class, you’ll dive into vector graphics and wearable design — making your own custom apparel, stickers, signs, and patches! Learn how to use professional design software to create bold, original graphics and then turn them into real products using vinyl cutters, embroidery, and direct-to-film printing. It’s your chance to design and wear your own ideas — or even start a brand!
courses.notes: Previously known as Design Studio II

courses.course_name: Intro to Wood and Metal Fabrication
courses.description: If you love to design, build, and make things that last, this is the class for you! In this hands-on course, you’ll explore how to design and create custom projects using wood, metal, and mixed materials. You’ll learn the basics of woodworking, welding, CNC routing, and CNC milling — and discover how digital design tools connect with real-world fabrication. From furniture to small product design, you’ll develop craftsmanship, creativity, and problem-solving skills while bringing your ideas to life in the shop.

Turn your ideas into reality — and maybe even a business! In this course, you’ll explore what it takes to launch a product, service, or brand. You’ll learn how to build a business plan, develop your brand identity, and use real design tools to prototype your ideas. Work in teams to pitch your project to local professionals and community partners, gain feedback, and connect your creativity to real-world opportunities. Whether you want to start a business, enter a pitch competition, or just learn how innovation works in the real world, this class gives you the skills and confidence to make it happen.
courses.prerequisites: 3D Design & Wearable Design
courses.notes: Offerings list shows course number 12053E

courses.description: Photography & Visual Storytelling at the Milton Innovation Center empowers students to explore the art and science of photography while developing technical skills and creative expression. Students will learn camera operation, composition, lighting, and photo editing, applying these skills across genres such as portrait, landscape, product, and photojournalism. With access to professional-grade equipment and editing software, students will create high-quality work for digital and print platforms and build a personal portfolio through hands-on projects and critiques. Guest speakers and workshops with professional photographers will offer real-world insights and career exploration opportunities. This course fosters artistic confidence and technical expertise, equipping students to communicate compelling visual stories in an increasingly image-driven world.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of Art 1
courses.notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

courses.description: This is a course offered to support students with acquiring their driver’s education permit. This class starts to explore the responsibilities that come with independent living and owning a vehicle by developing transferable skills and worker traits. Students also learn about other forms of transportation (biking, bus, taxi services, car-pooling, etc.) and determine which is their most viable option.
courses.credits_text: .5 (One Quarter or One Semester Alternate Days)

courses.description: The course is designed to provide students with the specific skills and competencies needed to be successful employees, advanced students, entrepreneurs, and leaders. The course helps students be informed and explore career education, planning and preparation beyond high school. Students explore the following need to know topics: career assessments, desired worker traits, worker rights, labor laws, job benefits, new employee paperwork, teaming & conflict, and professional communication.

The course is designed to provide students with the specific skills and competencies needed to be successful employees, advanced students, entrepreneurs, and leaders. The course helps students prepare and reflect on the application process, understand new employee paperwork, and polish their image in the work world. Students explore the following need to know topics: future planning, networking, application process & timeline, new employee paperwork, resume, cover letter, interview skills, and professional appearance.

Students are provided the opportunity to gain work experience in a local company with the on-site guidance of our school’s job coach or Work-Based Learning Coordinator. Company sites are selected by the Work-Based Learning Coordinator, can vary per quarter, and are meant to meet local company needs rather than necessarily match student interest. Coaching is provided through the application, training and working process with time to self-assess and reflect on each day. Students can earn up to two academic credits. Students will be required to fill out a Work Agreement Plan outlining learning objectives and meet with the Work Based Learning Coordinator or Employment Specialist for a mid-point and final evaluation.
courses.prerequisites: Grades 11-12. Enrolled in or completing Work After Education.
courses.notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION; Requires two blocks to account for transportation; program

courses.description: Students can earn up to two academic credits by documenting hours of employment and showing new learning. This must be approved through your School Counselor or Work-Based Learning Coordinator before you begin earning credit. Students will be required to fill out a Work Agreement Plan outlining learning objectives and meet with the Work Based Learning Coordinator, School Counselor or Employment Specialist for a mid-point and final evaluation. Students will also be assigned one discussion question and challenge learning task to complete each week.
courses.prerequisites: Grades 11-12. Enrolled in or completing Work After Education.
courses.notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION; program

courses.description: Internship/Service Learning provides each Milton High School student the opportunity to design and carry out a personally meaningful educational experience. This experience includes making connections with the community beyond school. Volunteering can help students gain confidence by giving them a chance to try something new and build a real sense of achievement. Volunteering can have a real and valuable positive effect on people, communities, and society in general and allow students the opportunity to learn new skills, gain experience and possible qualifications. Through volunteering students can challenge themselves to try something different, achieve personal goals, practice using their skills and discover hidden talents. This graduation requirement's guiding principle is that all students must demonstrate the ability to research a subject of their own choosing, take part in a meaningful internship or service project directly related to that subject, and demonstrate learning through keeping a record of learning and the creation of a final presentation. Exploration of a student’s internship/service learning may begin in the first year of advisory. Students will map out interests and begin exploring opportunities for completion of the project. Requirements include: 1. Meeting with the Service-Learning coordinator to discuss possibilities for the internship/service experience and to finalize logistics and details. Students will complete the preparation form and have the contract signed by parents/guardians and the site coordinator. 2. Completion of 30 hours of internship/service experience dedicated to the project. 3. Presentation of the project to their Teacher Advisory group and the Service-Learning Coordinator along with a written reflection of the experience. Students may begin this at any time during their high school career and must be fully completed by January of a student’s year of graduation. A student’s written reflection and presentation must be completed within one quarter from when the hours are completed.
courses.fulfills_text: Service Learning/Internships .5 Credit
courses.notes: program
program; Parent Conferences Fall & Spring; Pass/Fail

courses.description: Dual Enrollment is ideal for high school students who are academically prepared for college-level courses. They will earn college credits while progressing toward high school graduation. The Dual Enrollment program allows Vermont public high school students to take two free college courses during their junior or senior year of high school. Students are eligible for two vouchers from the end of sophomore year until graduation. Remedial courses are not eligible to be covered by a voucher. Textbooks, lab fees, comprehensive fees, and other materials and supplies are not covered by the voucher and are the responsibility of the student/family.* Final grades for the course will be Pass/Fail and will not be included in GPA and class rank, but will appear on the student’s high school transcript and be awarded one credit. If you want to have a letter grade included for your high school transcript, you must make that determination before the class begins.
courses.notes: program; two vouchers per student; Pass/Fail unless letter grade chosen before the class begins

courses.description: CCV offers a course entitled “Introduction to College & Careers (ICC).” ICC is a free, non-credit course for 9-12 students that helps them identify their interests and abilities, set goals for the future that align with their PLP’s, and develop skills for being successful in college and employment. CCV offers ICC courses every semester.

courses.description: Students spend their final year of high school at a Vermont College or University earning college credits that help them graduate from high school and get a jump-start on a college degree, tuition-free (not including textbooks and fees). Students in this program enroll full-time by taking four or five college-level classes during the fall and spring of their senior year for a total of up to 30 credits.
courses.provider: Community College of Vermont or Vermont State University campuses
courses.notes: program; students are no longer enrolled at Milton High School during Early College; up to 30 college credits

courses.description: Are you interested in exploring new courses and diving into interesting topics? Through our partnership with VHS Learning, Milton High School students now have access to 250+ unique course offerings that go beyond the traditional classroom. This program expands students’ learning options and can connect students from across the country and the world. With courses like Forensic Science, Principles of Investing, Veterinary Medicine, American Sign Language, Fashion Design, Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, and AP® Chinese Language and Culture, there are options for everyone! VHS Learning offers high school core, elective, Advanced Placement®, initial credit paced, and self-paced courses.
courses.notes: program; catalog lists 250+ VHS Learning courses; individual online courses not named except examples (Forensic Science, Principles of Investing, Veterinary Medicine, American Sign Language, Fashion Design, Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity, AP Chinese Language and Culture)
